chapters.title: Find businesses that need a website
chapters.goal: Identify a specific list of local businesses with no website or a badly outdated one — your warmest possible leads.
explanation: Search local businesses on a maps app in categories like barbers, tutors, bakeries, small repair shops — businesses that clearly still rely on word-of-mouth and foot traffic alone.

A business with NO website link listed, or a broken/very outdated-looking one, already knows on some level they need this — that awareness makes the pitch much easier than convincing someone from zero.
Build a shortlist of 10-15 such businesses in your area, noting what's missing on each (no site, no menu/price info, no contact form, not mobile-friendly).
Pick 2-3 to focus on first rather than trying to pitch all fifteen at once — quality of pitch beats quantity of targets.
Write a one-sentence value promise: "A real website with your hours, services and contact info, live in one week."
chapters.example: Dor searched "barber" on a local maps app, found six shops with no website link at all, and shortlisted the two closest to his neighborhood to approach first with a real, unsolicited demo.
mistakes: Pitching businesses that already have a good, modern website — a much harder sell than one with an obvious, visible gap.
Trying to approach fifteen businesses with the same generic effort instead of focusing on 2-3 with a strong, specific pitch.
Not noting exactly what's missing on each prospect's current presence before reaching out.
chapters.template:
Lead-finding worksheet:
Business category targeted: ____
Businesses found with no/outdated website: ____
What's missing on each (list): ____
Top 2-3 to approach first: ____
One-sentence value promise: "____"
checklist: Searched local businesses in a category likely to need this
Built a shortlist of 10-15 businesses with no/outdated websites
Noted exactly what's missing on each prospect
Picked 2-3 to focus on first

chapters.title: Understand what the business owner actually needs
chapters.goal: Know exactly what information and features a small business owner's customers actually look for, before building anything.
explanation: Small business website needs are usually simple and consistent: hours, location, contact info, services/menu/prices, and photos — not complex custom features.
Look at what similar successful local businesses' websites include, to understand the real baseline expected in that category.
Consider the business owner's OWN comfort level too — will they need to update this themselves later, or rely on you? That affects what platform/complexity makes sense.
Write a short brief: the business's core info, what a customer visiting the site would want to find fastest, and the owner's likely comfort with maintaining it.
If you get a chance to talk to the owner before building, ask directly what's frustrated them about not having a good site so far.
chapters.example: Dor noticed local barbershop sites that worked well all led with hours, a simple price list, and a "book now" contact button above the fold — so that became the standard structure for every site he built in this category.
mistakes: Overbuilding with unnecessary complex features the business and its customers don't actually need.
Not considering whether the owner needs to update the site themselves later.
Skipping research on what successful similar businesses' sites actually include.
chapters.template:
Business brief:
Core info needed: hours ____, location ____, services/prices ____, contact ____
What customers want to find fastest: "____"
Owner's comfort with updating it themselves: ____
checklist: Identified the core info every visitor to this site type needs
Researched successful similar businesses' site structure
Considered the owner's comfort level with future updates
Wrote a short brief before starting to build

chapters.title: Price the build and ongoing hosting
chapters.goal: Set a fair one-time build price, plus decide whether to offer ongoing hosting/updates as recurring income.
explanation: A one-time build fee is the core price — research typical rates for a simple small-business site to set a realistic starting number.
Consider a separate, smaller monthly fee for hosting and occasional updates — this turns one-time projects into a source of recurring income across multiple clients.
Keep pricing simple and clearly scoped: what's included (number of pages, revisions, timeline) at the stated price, with anything extra priced separately.
Factor in any real costs (a domain name, hosting if not free-tier) when calculating your actual margin, especially if you're covering these upfront.
Decide your price before pitching, not during the conversation — a confident, pre-decided price is easier to say clearly than one improvised on the spot.
chapters.example: Dor's package: "$250 one-time build, up to 5 pages, 2 revision rounds, live in one week — plus optional $25/month for hosting and small updates." Clear, and the monthly piece became steady income across several clients.
mistakes: No clear scope attached to the price, leading to endless "just one more change" requests.
Never offering the ongoing hosting/update fee, missing an easy source of recurring income.
Improvising a price on the spot during the pitch instead of deciding it beforehand.
chapters.template:
Pricing plan:
One-time build fee: $____ (pages/revisions/timeline included)
Monthly hosting/update fee: $____
Real costs to cover (domain/hosting): $____
checklist: Set a clear, scoped one-time build price
Decided whether to offer a monthly hosting/update fee
Factored in real domain/hosting costs
Decided the price before pitching, not during

chapters.title: Tools and startup costs
chapters.goal: Confirm you can build a real demo for free, and know the small costs involved in actually going live for a client.
explanation: AI website builders with free tiers can produce a full, real demo site from a short description — this is usually enough to pitch with, at zero cost.
The main real costs come once a client says yes: a domain name (usually $10-20/year) and possibly hosting beyond a free tier, depending on the builder used.
Decide upfront whether the client pays for their own domain/hosting directly, or whether you cover it and bill them (simpler to have them pay directly, avoiding you fronting costs).
Avoid paying for a premium website-builder plan before having a paying client who justifies the ongoing cost.
If a parent's card is needed for any tool or domain purchase, agree the amount and reimbursement plan together first.
chapters.example: Dor built free demo sites for his first two prospects entirely on a free-tier AI website builder, and had the client pay for their own $14/year domain directly rather than Dor fronting that cost.
mistakes: Paying for a premium website-builder plan before landing any paying client.
Fronting domain/hosting costs for a client instead of having them pay directly, creating unnecessary financial risk.
Building demos that require paid features before confirming a free tier can't do the job.
chapters.template:
Startup cost sheet:
Builder tool (free tier limits): ____
Domain cost (who pays): $____ / year — payer: ____
Hosting beyond free tier needed? Yes/No
checklist: Confirmed a free-tier builder can produce a real demo
Decided who pays for domain/hosting costs directly
Avoided paid builder plans before a real paying client
Agreed any spending with a parent if their card is used

chapters.title: Build credibility with a real sample
chapters.goal: Show up to a pitch with something finished, not just a description of what you could build.
explanation: Build a free, real demo site for one specific business (ideally one of your actual prospects) before ever pitching — a finished example converts far better than any verbal pitch.
Make a simple one-page portfolio or profile showing 1-2 demo sites, your package price, and a short line about why you do this (local businesses deserve a real online presence).
Use your own professional, working contact info and a clear way to reach you — building trust as a young business owner starts with basic professionalism.
Once you have a real paying client, ask permission to use their finished site as a portfolio example for future pitches.
Keep your portfolio focused on your best 2-3 examples rather than every site you've ever touched.
chapters.example: Dor built a complete demo site for one of his shortlisted barbershops — unsolicited, using only public info about their hours and services — and brought it to the pitch already finished rather than describing what he could build.
mistakes: Pitching with no demo or sample at all, relying only on a description of skills.
Not asking permission to showcase a finished client site in future portfolios.
An unprofessional first contact (no clear way to reach you, casual/unclear communication) for a service built on trust.
chapters.template:
Credibility builder:
Demo site built (for a real or realistic prospect): ____
One-page portfolio: done? Yes/No
Professional contact info ready? Yes/No
checklist: Built at least one real, unsolicited demo site before pitching
Made a simple portfolio/profile to share
Set up clear, professional contact info
Got permission to showcase completed client work

chapters.title: Pitch with the finished demo
chapters.goal: Present the free demo to the business owner and get a clear yes/no on moving forward.
explanation: Show up (in person if possible, or with a clear message) with the finished demo already built — "I made this for you, take a look" is far more compelling than "I could build you a website."
Keep the pitch short: what you noticed was missing, what you built, and your clear price for making it live under their own domain.
Be ready to answer the obvious question — "why should I trust a teenager with this" — with your portfolio and the demo itself as the answer, not defensiveness.
If the owner says not now, leave the demo link with them anyway and follow up politely once, a few weeks later — circumstances change.
Track which pitch approach and which business types actually convert, to focus effort efficiently as you approach more prospects.
chapters.example: Dor showed the barbershop owner the finished demo on his phone in person, said "this could be live under your own name in a week for $250," and got a yes on the spot — the finished demo did most of the convincing before he said a word about price.
mistakes: Pitching without the demo actually finished and ready to show.
Being defensive about age instead of letting the finished, professional work speak for itself.
Never following up with a prospect who said "not now," losing a lead that might convert later.
chapters.template:
Pitch plan:
Demo ready to show: Yes/No
Pitch script (short): "____"
Follow-up plan if "not now": ____
checklist: Brought a finished demo to the pitch, not just a description
Kept the pitch short and confident
Had a clear answer ready for trust/age concerns
Planned a polite follow-up for any "not now" responses

chapters.title: Close the deal and agree scope in writing
chapters.goal: Turn a yes into a signed, clear agreement before building the final version.
explanation: Put the agreement in writing, even briefly: price, what's included (pages, revisions), timeline, and who owns the domain and content afterward.
Clarify domain ownership explicitly — the business should own their own domain (registered in their name or a name they control), not one locked to your account.
Agree what happens if the client wants to leave or switch providers later — this builds trust and is simply fair, especially for a new, unproven working relationship.
Set a realistic delivery timeline (roughly a week is reasonable for a simple small-business site) and communicate proactively if anything will be late.
Get a deposit or full payment upfront or on delivery, agreed clearly in the written scope, rather than an informal "pay me whenever."
chapters.example: Dor's one-page agreement with the barbershop covered the $250 price, 5 pages, 2 revisions, one-week delivery, domain registered in the owner's own name, and payment due on delivery — signed by both before he touched the final build.
mistakes: Starting the final build on a verbal agreement with nothing written down.
Registering the client's domain under your own account instead of theirs, creating an ownership problem later.
No clear payment timing agreed, leading to awkward collection later.
chapters.template:
Agreement checklist:
Price and scope in writing? Yes/No
Domain registered in client's name? Yes/No
Delivery timeline: ____
Payment timing: ____
checklist: Got the agreement in writing before final build
Confirmed the domain is registered in the client's own name
Set a realistic delivery timeline
Agreed clear payment timing

chapters.title: Deliver, connect the domain, and support the launch
chapters.goal: Get the finished site live under the client's own domain and make sure they know how to use it going forward.
explanation: Connect the client's domain to the finished site carefully, testing it fully (all pages, contact forms, mobile view) before telling them it's live.
Walk the owner through anything they'll need to do themselves (checking a contact form inbox, requesting future changes) so they're not confused after launch.
Fix any launch-day issues fast — a broken link or form on day one is the worst possible first impression for a paying client.
If you offered ongoing hosting/updates, make sure the client clearly understands what's included in that monthly fee versus what counts as a new, separately-priced project.
Ask for a review or referral once the site has been live and working well for a couple of weeks, not immediately at launch.
chapters.example: Dor tested every page and the contact form on both desktop and phone before telling the barbershop owner it was live, then sent a short video walking through where to check for new contact-form messages.
mistakes: Announcing the site as live without fully testing it first, including on mobile.
Leaving the owner confused about how to check for messages or request future changes.
Asking for a review immediately at launch instead of after it's been live and working for a while.
chapters.template:
Launch checklist:
Domain connected and tested (all pages, forms, mobile)? Yes/No
Owner walkthrough done? Yes/No
Ongoing fee scope explained clearly? Yes/No
checklist: Fully tested the live site including mobile before announcing it
Walked the owner through how to use/maintain it
Fixed any launch-day issues quickly
Clarified what's included in any ongoing monthly fee

chapters.title: Getting paid
chapters.goal: Collect the build fee and any recurring hosting fee safely and legally.
explanation: Most payment methods for client invoicing (bank transfer, invoicing tools, PayPal) require an 18+ account holder — under that age, a parent's account handles this.
Use a simple invoicing tool (many have free tiers) for a professional record of what's owed and paid.
Agree the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent before the first client payment arrives.
For recurring hosting fees, set a clear, consistent monthly billing date so it doesn't become awkward or forgotten.
Follow up promptly and professionally on any late payment.
chapters.example: Dor's father's account received client payments via a free invoicing tool, with the one-time build fee invoiced on delivery and any monthly hosting fee billed on the 1st of each month.
mistakes: Not agreeing a clear payment schedule for both the one-time fee and any recurring fee.
Using a payment method without checking its age requirement.
Letting a late payment go unaddressed instead of a prompt, polite follow-up.
chapters.template:
Payment setup record:
Payment method/account holder (18+ if needed): ____
Build fee payment timing: ____
Recurring fee billing date (if any): ____
checklist: Confirmed the payment method's age requirement
Set clear payment timing for the one-time build fee
Set a consistent billing date for any recurring fee
Agreed the transfer arrangement with the account-holding parent
chapters.parentNote: Client invoicing and payment collection generally require an 18+ account holder for the bank/payment method involved. A parent needs to hold this under this age.

chapters.title: Accounting and taxes
chapters.goal: Track build fees and recurring hosting income, and understand what's owed.
explanation: Website-building income (both one-time build fees and recurring hosting fees) is taxable business income in almost every country, including for minors, with specifics that vary by country.
Keep a log per client: build fee, date paid, and any recurring monthly fee — separating one-time from recurring income helps you see your real predictable income.
Set aside a portion of income (a rough 20-25% placeholder is common) rather than spending it all as it arrives.
Track any real costs you covered (if any) — like a domain you fronted and got reimbursed for — separately from your actual profit.
Have one real conversation with a parent, and once income is more than occasional, check your country's actual rules for minors' business income.
chapters.example: Dor's spreadsheet had one column for one-time build fees and another for recurring monthly hosting fees, making it easy to see his growing predictable monthly income as he added clients.
mistakes: Mixing one-time and recurring income together, losing visibility into real predictable monthly income.
Not tracking reimbursed costs (like a fronted domain fee) separately from actual profit.
Spending all income immediately with nothing set aside.
chapters.template:
Income log (one row per client):
Client | Build fee | Date paid | Recurring fee | Running monthly recurring total
Set-aside plan: ____% saved so far: $____
checklist: Started a running income log separating one-time and recurring fees
Set aside a percentage of income
Tracked any reimbursed costs separately from profit
Had one conversation with a parent about this income
chapters.parentNote: Website-building income, including recurring hosting fees, is taxable in most places, including for minors. This needs a parent involved and a real check with local tax rules once income is meaningful.

chapters.title: Growing your client base
chapters.goal: Turn one successful build into a small, growing roster of clients with steady recurring income.
explanation: Ask happy clients for referrals directly — local business owners often know other local business owners, and a personal recommendation is powerful.
Use each finished site as a new, real portfolio example, making your next pitch even more convincing than the last.
Watch your recurring hosting income grow as a percentage of total income — it's the most stable part of this business and worth actively encouraging every client to opt into.
Know your realistic capacity for build timelines as you take on more clients, and don't overcommit past what you can deliver well and on time.
Review monthly: number of clients, recurring monthly income, and referral sources — a strong referral rate is often the clearest sign the business model is working.
chapters.example: After the barbershop, Dor got two referrals from that same owner within a month. He kept every client's demo in his growing portfolio and watched his recurring hosting income slowly become a meaningful steady base as he added clients.
mistakes: Never asking for referrals despite having happy, satisfied clients.
Taking on more build projects than can realistically be delivered well and on time.
Not tracking recurring hosting income separately, missing how it's becoming the more stable part of the business.
chapters.template:
Monthly growth review:
Active clients: ____  Recurring monthly income: $____
Referrals received this month: ____
Capacity check — realistic to take on another build right now? Yes/No
checklist: Asked at least one happy client for a referral
Added the latest finished site to my portfolio
Tracked recurring hosting income as a growing share of total income
Checked realistic capacity before committing to a new build
